evidence.field: 小 headword; PDF p. 76, printed p. 64
evidence.text: The entry calls 小 pictographic and interprets its marks as tiny dust or sand particles, an early graph of 沙. It says the graph was extended to mean ‘small,’ opposite 大, and cites oracle-bone and bronze uses, including 《粹》1004 小雨. It also describes extensions to low status, contempt and youth, and says the bronze form had become corrupted, prompting Shuowen’s 八-plus-丨 explanation. Both attached page images were inspected; the printed headword, cited forms 小, 沙, 大, 八, 丨 and 《粹》1004 are legible. This verifies the author’s account, not the disputed sand interpretation.

evidence.source: 李學勤主編,《字源》, 天津古籍出版社／遼寧人民出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692
evidence.field: Adjacent 少 entry; PDF p. 76 and continuation p. 77, printed pp. 64–65
evidence.text: The adjacent 少 entry says 小 and 少 were originally one graph and were used alike in oracle-bone texts, then differentiated; it describes 少’s final diagonal stroke as a distinguishing mark. The entry continues onto printed p. 65. Both source scans were inspected; the relevant 少 and 小 forms are legible. This is the book author’s graphic account, not proof of a historical sound relationship.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 小, 少 and 沙 records: formation, cited uses and graph components
evidence.text: The 小 record presents two analyses of its early marks: abstract dots for smallness, attributed to 商承祚 and 于省吾, or an early graph of 沙 depicting fine sand grains, attributed to 馬敍倫. It reports 小雨, 小食 as an afternoon expression, 小采 as a dusk expression, and bronze uses including 小鼎, 小子 and 小臣, without absolute artifact dates. Its 少 record says early forms could overlap and that three-dot and four-dot spellings later distinguished 小 and 少. The 沙 account reports competing analyses of bronze uses, so the cited pages do not establish a phonetic borrowing of 沙 from 小.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析—小

evidence.source: 中央研究院, Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The database asserts that 少 and 小 were originally one graph depicting fine sand grains, with ‘small’ as the original meaning, and says the lowest dot of 少 became a diagonal stroke in bronze inscriptions. This supports that interpretation as a source-attributed account; CUHK presents competing analyses of 小’s marks.
evidence.title: 漢字「少」：字形演變

evidence.source: 中央研究院, Academia Sinica Character Database
evidence.text: The page labels oracle-bone, bronze, small-seal and Shuowen forms. It interprets the earlier marks as scattered fine sand grains expressing smallness and says the middle dot became a vertical stroke separating the two side marks in small-seal script. This is the database’s interpretation, not independent proof of the marks’ referent.
evidence.title: 漢字「小」：字形演變

evidence.source: Masaki Nohara, “The reconstruction of the word shao (少) in Old Chinese Phonology,” 中国語学 262 (2015), pp. 57–75
evidence.field: 少–小 phonetic relationship and early orthographic usage, especially PDF pp. 59–65
evidence.text: Nohara reviews competing Old Chinese analyses. Zhengzhang and Pan allow links among 少, 小 and related forms via proposed nasal initials, while Schuessler and Baxter–Sagart reject a 少–小 phonetic-series relation in the discussion Nohara cites. Nohara argues that excavated-text spelling and sound evidence do not warrant treating the early graphic overlap as proof of a phonetic relationship. The paper also documents that 少 and 小 spellings could represent both ‘few’ and ‘small’ in some early materials, with regional and period differences.
evidence.title: 「少」の上古音について／The reconstruction of the word shao (少) in Old Chinese Phonology

gaps: The earliest marks’ referent remains disputed: consulted accounts describe abstract marks for smallness or fine sand grains. No inspected evidence independently establishes the depicted object or a phonetic borrowing of 沙 based on its name.

The 《字源》 entry reports oracle-bone 小雨 with 《粹》1004, but no inscription facsimile or absolute artifact date was checked. The consulted sources report time and status uses without establishing their dates or semantic bridges from ‘small.’

The shared-graph and later differentiation account for 小 and 少 is reported by several references, but it does not itself establish a historical sound relationship. Nohara’s inspected study finds the phonetic connection unsupported by the evidence he examines; the broader lexical relationship remains unsettled.
CUHK reports 小 as a sound component in 雀. This research did not establish that role through an independent historical sound comparison, so it remains source-attributed.
The WorldCat catalogue URL was not inspected. Edition details are from the supplied source registration; the source scans themselves were directly inspected.
